To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the liver conversion of docosohexaenoic (DHA) and arachidic (AA) acids from their respective 18 carbon precursors, α-LNA (DHA) or linoleic (AA) acid, in rats on a diet adequate in α-LNA but deficient in DHA was quantified.

liver conversion of DGA and other n- 3 PUFAs was much higher than conversion of AA from LA, and that the net daily secretion rate (ND) of DHA, ND = 20.3 μmol/day, was 50-fold greater than the reported brain DGA consumption rate of 0.4 μmol/day.
the liver can convert dietary α-LNA to DHA and that the liver can supply DHA for brain consumption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis of the essential fatty acids (EPA, DHA and AA) in the liver of rats from the dietary precursors α-linolenate and linolate.
the conversion of α-linolenate to long-chain n- 3 PUFA, and the role of dietary long-chain n-6 and n-3 PUFAs in the regulation of this process in rats.
understanding the mechanisms of long-chain n-6 and n-3 fatty acid biosynthesis and the factors that influence these processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the liver can synthesize EPA and DHA from α-linolenate in the absence of dietary DHA, and that this conversion is sufficient to meet brain DHA requirements in humans.
the liver can convert α-LNA into DHA at a rate sufficient to meet brain DHA requirements, and the rate of DHA conversion is greater than the rate of AA conversion.
the liver can convert α-LNA to DHA, but the conversion rate is not sufficient to meet the brain's daily requirement of DHA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the liver is a major site for the biosynthesis of EPA and DGA from their 18-C precursors in rats fed an adequate α-LNA-containing but DHA-free diet.

the liver can efficiently convert dietary α-LNA to DHA and EPA, and that the liver can supply the entire body with sufficient DHA for brain and retinal development, maintenance and function, and other physiological processes.
the liver of the rat can maintain brain metabolism of n-3 PUFAs with an adequate supply of α-LNA alone.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver can convert α-LNA into EPA and DHA, and the rate of this conversion is sufficient to meet the daily requirements of the brain for DHA.
the liver can convert α-LNA to DHA at an efficient rate, and this may be sufficient to maintain brain DHA synthesis in vegetarians or those on n-3 PUFAs adequate diets.
the liver can synthesize EPA and DHA from dietary α-linolenate, even when DHA is absent from the diet.
